title: Trinkets
summary: Minor enchanted objects that hold no working Sphere Effect.

claims.text: A Trinket has odd properties set into it when made, yet it does not use the Spheres afterward; the name is only a handy label, not one mages use.
Life, Matter and Forces can grow, toughen or retune an ordinary object, and Quintessence can consecrate it, turning it into a small Wonder.
A Trinket is built of one or two plain materials and does one simple job, such as silence or turning bullets; a gun can qualify, but a car or a computer cannot.
Wonders reshape reality, so they can build Paradox; how much depends on whether the use looks coincidental or vulgar and whether Sleepers see it.
A machine makes strange results easier to accept in mass-media cultures, so technological Wonders often pass as coincidence.
Some symbols, like a priest raising a cross, are so rooted in public belief that they may count as coincidental in the right setting.

title: Resonance and Synergy
summary: How a mage's energetic signatures combine.

claims.text: When Resonance and Synergy share a flavour their dots add together, when they clash the smaller is taken from the larger, and when unrelated the one that fits the moment supplies the pool.
Resonance colours the people, places and Backgrounds around a mage, such as Allies, Chantry, Sanctum, Totem and Avatar.
Resonance can decide whose magick counts as coincidental and whose as vulgar inside a Sanctum, Chantry or Realm.

title: Chantry and sect feuds
summary: The grudges that split mage groups.

claims.text: Feuds can cross factions, like a Hermetic House against a Progenitor lab, or sit inside one, like two Etherite collectives at odds.
Rival alchemist sects have quarrelled for centuries over which of them may claim the name Solificati.
A mage who offends a whole sect within a larger group faces +2 difficulty on social rolls with its members, though they stop short of murder.

title: Paradigm: consciousness first
summary: The belief that mind, not matter, is what is real.

claims.text: Followers point to pain, colour and memory as real yet without material form, and to the Digital Web as proof that the physical is not all there is.
The view tends to draw the Mercurial edge of the Virtual Adepts, esoteric Etherites and tech-minded Ecstatics.

title: Paradigm: the coming threshold
summary: The creed that the present world is ending and a new one will follow.

claims.text: Believers read the shift as End Times, a Singularity, a leap in human evolution, the return of the Ancestors or the close of the Kali Yuga.
Western alchemists frame it as dissolution, separation and conjunction, so the creed is strong among Solificati of the Order of Hermes and the Disparates.

title: Ancestor veneration
summary: Honouring the dead for their favour and protection.

claims.text: The honoured dead are held to guard descendants who tend them and to bring bad luck when ignored.
It stands between a paradigm and a practice: shrines, daily homage, feast days such as Dia de Muertos, offerings, and keeping their memory safe.
Such rites may serve as Fetters for ancestral ghosts, while using necromancy on one's own forebears is thought a grave wrong.

title: Paradigm: no limits
summary: Approaching every boundary without fear in order to become divine.

claims.text: Drawn from the Sanskrit idea of aghora, the devotee meets all limits without terror and so knows Creation as a god does.
Nephandi hold this view, but a few Akashayana and Chakravanti walk it in deep secrecy, and Gnostic and Hermetic antinomian practice echoes it.
The Technocracy loathes it, while Traditions and Disparates put up with milder forms so long as the mage causes no trouble.

title: Paradigm: back to the wild
summary: The creed that civilisation weakens humanity.

claims.text: Extreme Verbenae, Dreamspeakers and Kopa Loei hold it, along with some anarcho-primitivist Ecstatics and Adepts.
Adherents keep tools and clothing to the barest minimum and shun cars, computers and other high technology.

title: Paradigm: the evolved elite
summary: The belief that the Enlightened have outgrown ordinary humans.

claims.text: It runs from old racial and caste claims, the Thule Society among them, to modern transhumanist and mutant theories.
Many Progenitors and Virtual Adepts, above all the Mercurial Elite, credit their gifts to being evolved or upgraded beyond the herd.

title: Justice in the Council of Nine
summary: How the Traditions police their own.

claims.text: The Council keeps its loose-cannon members in check through protocols and penalties that are often applied unevenly.
Gilgul shatters a guilty mage's Awakened soul into fragments and ends that Awakening for good, even if the body lives.
Debate over the Ascension Warrior has left Council mages unsure that Gilgul is final, since shattered souls may rejoin in one body.
Charges against an operative are ranked primary, secondary and tertiary, and the primary one weighs most in judging intent and penalty.
Abuse of Office covers misuse of rank or reckless hypertech near the Masses; Collaboration covers close ties with Reality Deviants that lack sanction.
Penalties include Forfeiture of Union Backgrounds, demotion, reassignment far from home, and reworking of the offender's loved ones.

title: The Union's ideals
summary: What visionary Technocrats still strive for.

claims.text: Beyond clones and weapons, Technocratic labs chase clean power, medicine, lasting farming, better materials and utopian forms of government.
Such Technocrats point to lighting, easy travel, steady food supplies and stable states as the Union's gifts to the world.

title: Law of the Disparate Alliance
summary: Courts and protectorates among the Crafts.

claims.text: The Crafts kept apart for centuries, care little for ideas of Ascension and dislike anyone who tries to rule their world.
Each member group names eight Wise Hearts, and at least one per group must be young or weak as a reminder of what justice owes the small.
An accused Ally gets three Advocates from the Wise Hearts, one for the accused, one for the victims and one for the Alliance, normally drawn from other groups.
Sleepers placed under a Craft's protection are off limits to other Crafts, and the protecting Craft must police them; the idea works better on paper than in practice.
Marauders reshape reality simply by being present and have no shared laws, leaders or ranks, so they are no true faction.
The Umbral Underground tries to weaken the Consensus by wrecking Technocratic and Nephandic operations.
Most Bai Dai groups had died out by the twenty-first century; by 2017 only the Maenads, the Hemlock Court, the Flowers of Camaxtli and the Fire of the Mahdi remain.
God's Left Hand, also called the Chaioth ha-Quadesh, rose around the millennium as a fierce cult of religious madness armed with magick and hypertech.
